name: allureofthestars
desc: Near-future Sci-Fi roguelike and tactical squad combat game
why: A near-future roguelike with tactical squad combat that is genuinely unusual for a terminal game.

brief.what_it_is: Allure of the Stars is a near-future science-fiction roguelike with tactical squad combat, written in Haskell on the LambdaHack engine. The player manually controls each member of a squad, though the homepage says the best tactic is often to scout with one character and let the others guard key areas. The game is turn-based but fine-grained: projectiles fly over time at varying speeds and can be sidestepped or shot down. It can be played in a browser at allureofthestars.com/play, and the Homebrew formula installs an executable called Allure.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as an attempt to make a roguelike that feels like a shared experience with a band of trusted friends, where players fight as one organism with minimal communication and build their own story. The homepage describes the UI as deliberately sparse so the player's imagination does most of the sensory work, "like when reading a book, but with less words and more action."
brief.how_it_works: The homepage lists the design differences from classic roguelikes. Factions and actors all obey the same rules (field of view, skill checks, equipment and terrain use), and combat is deterministic, with randomness coming only from AI decisions and procedural generation. There is almost no HP regeneration, and each character has 10 equipment slots. Each faction has one shared, unlimited inventory that sits at a physical place on the map and can be ransacked. Several levels advance simultaneously while others are frozen, and all are persistent.
brief.install_notes: Homebrew installs the Allure executable. The homepage also offers official binaries for Linux and Windows, a Homebrew formula with Mac OS X binaries, and a browser version at http://allureofthestars.com/play, which needs no install. The README and manual were not reachable, so no configuration or first-run steps are known.
brief.standout: Few terminal or roguelike games combine real-time-feeling projectile flight, per-character tactical control of a squad, deterministic combat, and faction inventories that exist as physical objects on the map. The homepage also says the same simulation rules apply to player and AI alike, which is an unusually strict design principle for the genre.
brief.status: Unknown for the latest release, since no release date or commit date was visible. The homepage footer reads "Copyright 2015-2021 Mikolaj Konarski", and it links to a dev channel, a Matrix room, a bug tracker and a changelog, so the project looks active at least through 2021. I could not reach the source repository to confirm recent commits; my guessed GitHub URLs returned 404.
brief.caveats: The source repository URL could not be confirmed, so I could not read a README or the changelog. The homepage says the author is pursuing goals like brain implant interfaces and aliens regretting plots against Earth, which read as tongue-in-cheek. The homepage does not list a licence. Official binaries are for Linux, Windows and Mac via Homebrew, but platform details beyond that are unknown. The homepage's own critics say it is hard to follow ("I have no idea what's going on"), so the learning curve may be steep.
quotes: "So that was a lot of fun, but *I have no idea what's going on*."
